name: Halo Effect
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: If the Founder Seems Brilliant, the Token Must Be Too: The Halo Effect
lesson.summary: The halo effect is the tendency for a positive impression in one area to bleed into unrelated judgments, letting a charismatic founder, a famous backer, or slick branding stand in for actual due diligence on a blockchain project.
lesson.body:
The halo effect was first named by psychologist Edward Thorndike in 1920, based on research showing that military officers who rated a soldier highly on one trait, such as physical bearing, also tended to rate that same soldier highly on unrelated traits like intelligence or leadership, as though one positive impression radiated outward and colored everything else. Later research, including studies by Richard Nisbett and Timothy Wilson in the 1970s, showed the same pattern with physical attractiveness: people rated as more attractive were also judged, with no supporting evidence, to be more intelligent, more competent, and more trustworthy. The defining feature of the halo effect is that the traits being conflated are logically independent, attractiveness has no bearing on intelligence, yet the impressions merge anyway.

The mechanism is a shortcut in impression formation: an overall favorable or unfavorable feeling toward a person or thing forms quickly, often from a single salient cue, and subsequent judgments about unrelated qualities get colored by that global feeling rather than assessed independently. It is closely related to the affect heuristic, the tendency to let an emotional reaction stand in for a more effortful, analytical judgment.

Blockchain fundraising leans on the halo effect constantly. A founder who is articulate, confident on stage, and has an impressive resume from a well known technology company generates a favorable overall impression, and that impression then bleeds into judgments about the project's tokenomics, security, and legal compliance, none of which the founder's presentation skills actually speak to. Celebrity endorsements and association with a prominent venture capital firm produce the same effect: the reasoning that a smart investor put money into this, so it must be sound, treats one party's due diligence, or lack of it, as a substitute for the listener's own. Investors have repeatedly poured money into projects on the strength of a compelling founder or a recognizable backer's name, only to discover afterward that the underlying code, governance structure, or business model had never actually been vetted on its own terms.

Design quality produces a similar effect on a smaller scale. A polished website, a well produced explainer video, and professional looking documentation create an impression of competence and legitimacy that has no necessary connection to whether the smart contract underneath has been audited or whether the token distribution is fair. Because visual polish is easy to produce and expensive smart contract audits are not, the correlation between how professional a project looks and how sound its actual code is can be weak or even inverted, since fraudulent projects have every incentive to invest heavily in appearances precisely because appearances are what most people evaluate.

Countering the halo effect requires deliberately separating the questions that got merged by a single impression: is the team credible, is the code sound, is the token structure fair, and is the legal and regulatory position defensible are four different questions that each deserve their own evidence, not one global impression applied across all four. Like appeal to novelty and anchoring bias, the halo effect is a specific, well documented instance of the broader category of cognitive bias, a shortcut that saves mental effort at the cost of accuracy, and naming it is often enough to prompt the more effortful, itemized evaluation that blockchain due diligence actually requires.
